newsitem.title: SPAIN: Telefonica share fever grips Spanish public.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica share fever grips Spanish public.

text.p: Strong demand for Telefonica shares has gripped the Spanish public, allowing Spain to boost the retail tranche and thus reduce the need for placing the rest with foreign institutions, analysts said on Tuesday.

State holding company SEPPa, which is selling its last 20.9 percent stake in the domestic telephone operator, said late on Monday it was lifting the proportion of shares offered to small investors -- the retail tranche -- by 17.1 million shares to 102.65 million.
This is 60 percent of the initial stake, up from 50 percent originally foreseen.

"There's plentiful demand for the domestic tranche, while at the international level it seems the placement is more difficult, so it doesn't surprise us they've upped the retail tranche," said a telecoms analyst at a Madrid brokerage.
SEPPa said it reserved the right to increase the retail tranche yet further before the end of the offer on February 14.
Shares offered to institutional investors abroad will now be 32 percent, or 54.74 million shares.

An aggressive publicity campaign aimed at encouraging the public to buy shares has been highly successful. Subscriptions so far have totalled 700 million shares, outstripping demand more than eight times, according to figures given last Friday.
Originally the retail tranche was 85.5 million shares, and Telefonica has had to tone down its promise to guarantee a minimum of 100 shares for every retail shareholder.
This possibility was included in the share prospectus, a Telefonica spokesman said.
Last night SEPPa also fixed the maximum price for the retail offer at just 40 pesetas below the stock's all-time high at 3,385 pesetas.
Dealers said they believed the stock had been well-managed in the run-up to the sale, making sure the government got a good price for the last tranche of the national operator.
"A lower price would have increased the attraction of buying Telefonica shares even more, but the demand is very strong (at these prices) in any case," said one analyst.
Analysts said they were expecting few cancellations in the run-up to the final date for definitive subscriptions.

But the success of the offer with investment institutions did not seem so resounding, analysts said. This explained why the firm had released no official indications of institutional demand, they added.

The high share price seems to have deterred institutions, coupled with a estimated price/earnings ratio of 16 times for 1997, compared with 13 times for other European operators. Added to this the stock markets are already awash with telecom shares after the Deutsche Telekom offer and with Italy's Stet due to come, they said.

"There'll be no problem placing 20.9 percent of Telefonica on the market, although on an international scale the stock isn't very cheap as there are alternatives for investors," said an analyst at a German bank.

For this reason Telefonica chairman Juan Villalonga has been keen to press home in interviews the idea that buying shares should be considered a medium- to long-term investment, rather than a quick buck in the short term.
